title: Washington and Canada
subtitle: Desert vineyards and ice wine
objectives: Explain how ice wine shaped Canada

steps.title: Washington
steps.body: Washington's vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, which block Pacific rain. The Columbia Valley is a desert, with under 200 mm of rain a year, so all vines are irrigated from rivers. Long summer days at 46 degrees north give ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling and Chardonnay lead.

steps.title: Cold winters and sandy soils
steps.body: Winter can drop below minus 20 degrees, damaging vines. Growers plant on slopes for air drainage and bury canes in some cases. Sandy, wind-blown soils mean phylloxera struggles, so most vines grow on their own roots. Walla Walla, Red Mountain and Yakima Valley are top AVAs.

steps.prompt: Which statements about Washington are true?
options: Most vineyards lie east of the Cascades
Many vines grow on their own roots
steps.explanation: Sandy soils keep phylloxera at bay, so own-rooted vines are common.

steps.title: Canada
steps.body: Canada's main regions are Ontario's Niagara Peninsula, moderated by Lake Ontario, and British Columbia's Okanagan Valley, a dry, warm valley in the interior. Reliable hard winters made Canada the world's leading ice wine producer, especially from Vidal and Riesling. The VQA system sets quality and origin rules.

steps.prompt: Which grape is widely used for Canadian ice wine?
steps.explanation: Vidal, a hardy hybrid, and Riesling are the main ice wine grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Washington's vineyards are an irrigated desert east of the Cascades
Cold winters and sandy soils mean many own-rooted vines
Canada leads in ice wine from Niagara and the Okanagan
